primitives.name: Referential Bias Index
primitives.verbatim_quote: Research question How do NFL fans' referring expressions (in-group "we/us" vs out-group "they/them" references to teams) shift as a function of live win probability during games?
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'RBI': 'dimensionless index, normalized to [0, 1]', 't': 'time in minutes since game start'}
primitives.assumptions: Fans' referential behavior is a stochastic process; in-group bias increases with home-team WP; out-group bias decreases with away-team WP.
primitives.breakdown_regime: At t=0, RBI ≈ 0.5; at t→∞, RBI converges to deterministic limit based on final outcome.

layer2.mapping: RBI encodes intergroup sentiment as a kernel-weighted average of pronoun usage over time.
layer2.telemetry: Comment-level binary classification accuracy of in-group vs out-group references.

primitives.name: Win Probability Correlation Slope
primitives.verbatim_quote: Best tagger applied to 100k comments; per-WP-bin reference rates regressed on WP to get slopes.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'\\text{slope}': 'unitless rate of change', '\\mathbb{E}[\\text{ref}]': 'expected reference rate (in-group or out-group)', '\\text{WP}': 'win probability in [0, 1]'}
primitives.assumptions: Reference rates vary linearly with WP within bins; slope captures directional sensitivity of language to outcome likelihood.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Slope approaches zero when WP stabilizes near 0 or 1; negative slope indicates increasing out-group bias with higher WP.

layer2.mapping: Slope maps to GSE's dynamic risk-adjusted sentiment signal, where positive slope implies increasing confidence in in-group.
layer2.telemetry: OLS regression coefficient from binned reference rates against WP.

primitives.name: Pronoun Resolution Accuracy
primitives.verbatim_quote: Method / model Two taggers map each comment to reference labels (none / in-group / out-group, plus pronoun-form subtypes like we[in], they[out]): - GPT-4o prompting, with WP supplied either numerically or linguistically ("the home team has a 70% chance of winning"), plus temperature scaling variants.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'\\text{Accuracy}': 'dimensionless score in [0, 1]', '\\hat{y}_i': 'predicted reference label', 'y_i': 'true reference label', '\\mathbb{I}(\\cdot)': 'indicator function'}
primitives.assumptions: Tagger performance is measured against expert annotations; accuracy reflects semantic fidelity of pronoun resolution.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Accuracy plateaus above 70% for both GPT-4o and Llama-3-8B under optimal conditions.

layer2.mapping: Accuracy serves as a proxy for linguistic coherence in GSE's pre-game text embedding pipeline.
layer2.telemetry: Macro-F1 score on held-out test set of 318 expert-labeled comments.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that referential bias (RBI) is a latent stochastic process governed by live win probability (WP). RBI evolves through time as a function of WP, forming a conditional distribution P(RBI|WP). The slope of expected reference rates against WP provides a first-order derivative measure of how sentiment shifts with outcome certainty. This is modeled as a linear regression over binned WP values, yielding a scalar slope parameter. However, since WP is the exogenous driver rather than a consequence of language, this relationship does not support predictive modeling for GSE’s win/spread/total systems. The paper's validation lacks out-of-sample forecasting tests, making its findings descriptive only. The derived kernel of referential dynamics fails to provide incremental signal beyond existing WP proxies such as nflFastR. Thus, while RBI may serve as an epistemic anchor for understanding crowd psychology, it cannot be used to forecast outcomes directly.
